subject: Glarmester Nordlys, a fictional glazier's workshop that cuts replacement panes to measure and prices them from the buyer's own two measurements.

colour.strategyWhy: The ground is float glass seen flat on in north light, which is a colour and not a neutral, and it is the material the whole business is about. A white page would have been a form about glass; this is a page made of it.

sources.name: glasflade
sources.material: 4 mm clear float glass laid flat and seen from above in north light, which is how a cut pane looks on the bench before it is wrapped
sources.why: The one material every order is made of. It is the page's ground because it is the workshop's.

sources.name: skaerebaenk
sources.material: the grey felt on the cutting bench
sources.why: Everything in the workshop is laid on the felt, so everything on the page that holds numbers is laid on it too: the price list and the specification.

sources.name: blyant
sources.material: the pencil line on a cutting docket
sources.why: The mark a glazier actually makes. Body text, headings and every measuring line are drawn in it.

sources.name: rudekant
sources.material: the green seen edge-on through the thickness of a sheet of float glass
sources.why: The only colour in the workshop that is not grey, and it is only visible at the edge, which is exactly where a glazier looks. It carries the action.

sources.name: linoliekit
sources.material: linseed putty, about two weeks old
sources.why: The warm note in an otherwise cold room. Used at low opacity behind the things that are about time rather than measurement.

sources.name: roedkridt
sources.material: the red chalk a glazier marks a bad cut with
sources.why: In the workshop it means stop. On the page it means the same thing and nothing else: the error state and the 2.200 mm limit on the bench drawing.

sources.name: friskkant
sources.material: the white of a freshly cut edge held to the light
sources.why: The only pure white in the palette, kept for what sits on the action.

primitives.from: derived: blyant at 34 per cent, for rules and hairlines that separate without speaking
derived: roedkridt at 9 per cent, the ground an error message sits on
derived: friskkant at 55 per cent, the chalked ground the docket itself is written on

pairs.name: body on the ground
pairs.use: every paragraph, heading and measurement on the page ground

pairs.name: body on the bench
pairs.use: the price list and the written specification, which are laid on the felt

pairs.name: the button
pairs.use: .skriv, the one action on the page

pairs.name: the button, hovered
pairs.use: .skriv:hover, which goes to pencil rather than lightening the green

pairs.name: the focus ring
pairs.use: :focus-visible, a 3px solid outline at 3px offset on the page ground

pairs.name: the focus ring on the button
pairs.use: .skriv:focus-visible. The outline sits at 3px offset, so it is painted on the docket panel behind the button and not on the button; it switches to pencil because a green ring on a green button is not a ring.

pairs.name: the error message
pairs.use: .fejl, the message under the field that caused it

pairs.name: the invalid field's edge
pairs.use: input[aria-invalid=true], a 3px bottom border in red chalk

pairs.name: a field's edge at rest
pairs.use: the bottom border of every number field, which is the field's only boundary

rest.changes: Nothing moves. A field is a pencil line under a number and nothing else: no box, no fill, no rounded corner, because a docket has ruled lines and not boxes.
rest.carriedBy: the line itself, at full pencil weight, and the label above it in the measuring face

focus.changes: A 3px solid outline in glass-edge green at 3px offset, and on the button it switches to pencil because a green ring on a green button is not a ring.
focus.carriedBy: the outline's own thickness and offset, which are visible with no colour perception at all

hover.changes: The button's ground goes from glass edge to pencil. It darkens rather than lightens, so it reads as pressing rather than as glowing.
hover.carriedBy: the change in lightness, which is 4.6 to 1 between the two grounds, plus the cursor

error.changes: The field's bottom border goes to red chalk at 3px, and a message appears under that field naming what is wrong in millimetres.
error.carriedBy: the border going from 1px to 3px, and the message's own text, which says the number and the limit

schemes.why: The use scene is a person standing at a broken window with a tape measure, in daylight, holding a telephone. The page is read once, in the light, next to the thing it is about. A dark scheme would be a second palette nobody in that scene ever sees, and the ground is a material rather than a neutral, so there is no dark equivalent of it that is still float glass.

colour.genericnessRisk: A pale grey-green ground with near-black text is arrivable at by anyone reaching for calm, and the ground alone would not identify this workshop. What a competitor cannot arrive at is the reason each colour is here: red chalk means stop because it means stop on the bench, and the green is edge-on glass rather than a brand green. The risk is that the reasons live in this file and the page only shows the values.

departures.from: the direction record names six materials
departures.why: The record counts the materials in the workshop. The contract counts the values the page needs, and two of them are the same materials with air in them: a hairline at 34 per cent and an error ground at 9 per cent. They are derived and say so.

roles.source: system, ships with Windows; the fallback stack carries the rest
roles.why: The DIN-derived condensed grotesque is the hand that writes measurements on a technical drawing. It is used for headings and for every number that is a measurement, and for nothing else, so a number set in it is a claim that it is a measured value.
roles.genericnessRisk: A condensed grotesque for headings is a common move. What is not common is restricting it to measurements, so the typeface itself carries the difference between a number that was measured and a number that was written down.

roles.source: system, ships with Windows; the fallback stack carries the rest
roles.why: A text serif with a large x-height, designed to be read on screen at small sizes. The workshop's own words, falsmaal and kitfals and sombelist, are set in a face that reads like a trade manual rather than like an interface.
roles.genericnessRisk: Georgia as a fallback is the most-used screen serif there is, so on a machine with neither Sitka nor Charter the page loses most of what makes its text look like a trade manual. The stress case measures exactly that.

scale.name: t0
scale.role: the smallest label on a measuring line

scale.name: t1
scale.role: captions, the error message, table cells

scale.name: t3
scale.role: the button, and a measurement in a field

scale.name: t5
scale.role: the total, and the second heading level, 38px from 900px

stress.case: a heading three times its expected length, in Danish
stress.expected: It wraps to three lines and the drawing below it moves down. Nothing is clipped and the bench drawing does not shrink, because the drawing's height is set from its own aspect ratio and not from the space left over.

stress.case: the page at 200 per cent zoom at 1440
stress.expected: The two columns become one, the same way they do at 375, because the layout switches on available width rather than on device. The bench drawing stays legible and its measuring numbers stay on their lines.

stress.case: the fallback stack, with Bahnschrift and Sitka Text both unavailable
stress.expected: Roboto Condensed and Georgia take over. The measuring numbers get wider, so the numbers sitting on the bench drawing's measuring lines are the case to check: they must stay on their lines and not overlap.

stress.case: aeoeaa and the Danish thousands separator, a full stop, in every face and size
stress.expected: 2.200 mm reads as two thousand two hundred and not as two point two, and ae, oe and aa render in both faces and in every fallback.

typography.genericnessRisk: Two system faces, no webfont, chosen for what they are rather than for what is fashionable. The risk is the opposite of the usual one: on a machine with neither face installed the page falls back to Segoe UI and Georgia, which is the most ordinary pair on the internet, and the whole typographic argument is carried by fonts that may not be there.

layout.path: See the bench and its 2,4 m limit, enter two measurements in millimetres, watch the pane draw itself onto the bench at the right proportion, choose a glass and a handover, read the total and the falsmaal, then write the cutting specification.
layout.grouping: Everything that is a measurement is on the bench drawing or in the specification, and both are laid on the felt. Everything that is a fact about the workshop, the week, the people, the address, is on the glass ground with nothing under it. A visitor can tell what is theirs and what is the workshop's by what it is lying on.
layout.densityWhy: A cutting docket is dense where the numbers are and empty everywhere else. The specification and the price list are packed; the bench drawing has air around it because a drawing needs room to be read as a drawing.

rhythm.base: 8px, which is the docket's own ruling

layout.topology: Two columns on the wide view: a drawing that owns the left and a form that owns the right, with the drawing taller than the form so the eye starts on the bench. Below the fold the page is one column of workshop facts, each a band on the glass ground, with the week drawn as its own figure. On narrow the drawing goes full width and the form comes under it, so the order of the argument is the order of the scroll.

firstViewportObject.what: The measured drawing of the cutting bench, with the 2.200 mm limit set off in red chalk, and the visitor's own pane drawn onto it in proportion as soon as the first measurement is typed.

signature.what: The same bench drawing: an SVG where the 2.200 mm is drawn once and for all and the visitor's pane is drawn onto it at the right proportion, with measuring lines and the numbers sitting on the lines.

responsive.becomes: One column. The bench drawing goes full width at the top and the form comes under it, so the reading order and the scroll order are the same. The drawing's measuring numbers drop from 72px to 19px and the tick weight from 4.5 to 1.2, because a drawing scaled down without redrawing its own annotation is a drawing nobody can read.
departures: the navigation is set two by two rather than wrapping three and one, because a wrapped three and one reads as a missing menu item

responsive.becomes: Still one column, and the drawing keeps its full width, but the measuring numbers go to 34px and the tick weight to 2.2. The price list becomes a real table rather than stacked rows.

Two columns. The drawing takes the left and roughly three fifths of the width; the form takes the right. The drawing is taller than the form, so the first thing the eye lands on is the bench and not the fields.
departures: the workshop's week is drawn at full width below, and is the only element that ignores the two-column grid, because a week is seven days across and not five sevenths of the page

layout.container: The content stops at 1240px and centres. Nothing goes edge to edge except the bands' own grounds, which run full width so a band reads as a surface rather than as a card. Past 1240px the page gains margin and nothing else grows, because a measuring drawing scaled past its own annotation is a picture of a drawing.

stress.case: empty, before any measurement is entered
stress.expected: The bench is drawn with its 2.200 limit and the pane is absent. The price area says what it will show rather than 0 kr, and the drawing reads as a bench waiting rather than as an image that failed to load.

stress.case: a measurement under 30 mm and one over 2.200 mm
stress.expected: The message appears under the field that caused it and names the falsmaal it would produce, or the 2,4 m bench. Nothing else on the page moves.

stress.case: the longest Danish glass name in the price list at 375
stress.expected: It wraps within its cell and the price stays on its own line, right aligned, still readable as a column of prices.

layout.squint: Out of focus the page is one large pale rectangle with a darker horizontal band across it, which is the bench, and a lighter block to its right, which is the form. That shape is the argument: the bench is the thing, and the form is what you do to it. If the form were the darker block the page would be a calculator with a picture of a bench next to it, which is a different and worse page.
